content_html_sanitized:
Analysis by Richard Cowan 

Yesterday, in response to questions in Parliament from members of the generally pro-legalization Labor Party, the Dutch Health Minister reconfirmed what MarijuanaNews.com has previously reported, that only tobacco smoking will be banned in coffee shops on July 1. 

See 

International “Prohibition Situation Report” – DEAland Media Ignore News Showing Cannabis Prohibition Is Counterproductive. Coffee Shop System Survives. 

This means that the practice of mixing cannabis and tobacco will no longer be allowed in the shops (and restaurants where cannabis use is permitted.) 

I saw the story yesterday on the Dutch News, but today it was even on Forbes.com in a story from Thomson Financial News 

There is actually a provision for the coffee shops to set up separate areas for customers who want to smoke their cannabis with tobacco, but – as is the case in other countries, the staff will not be allowed to go there. 

Thompson reported that Klink will examine the ban's effect on coffee shops around the first of the year, but I doubt if many of the shops will bother with the separate areas, simply because most are too small. 

Ironically, the Dutch sometimes refer to pure cannabis joints as “American” – because – like most Europeans – the Dutch first started smoking cannabis as hashish sprinkled in hand-rolled tobacco cigarettes. The Dutch have a very high rate of paper sales, but some of them just use it for tobacco. (Really) 

The pragmatic approach shown by the Dutch may or may not always yield the best outcome, but it does demonstrate why I am confident that the coffee shop system will prevail, especially in Amsterdam and a few other cities. 

See 

Challenging the UN’s Lying Drug Czar. Why We Owe The Dutch So Much and Why I Am Proud to Have Dr. Polak As A Friend. See It On YouTube! 

Of course, the Dutch do have their problems, even with cannabis policies. 

First, despite pressure from the mayors of the major cities and many in the police hierarchy, the politicians still cannot get up the nerve and/or gumption to “legalize” – tolerate – the supply-side, what they call the backdoor. 

See

Dutch Developments: Police Union Protests Cannabis Policies. Farmers Diversify. Mayors and Police Chiefs Call for UN Policy Review. Only In Holland. 

The other problem they have with cannabis comes from retail buying by its neighbors near Dutch border cities. Sometimes the Belgian and German politicians make noises, but the real problem is the noise and traffic caused by Belgians and Germans coming just across the border to buy weed. 

Recently, the mayor of Maastricht , which is on a thin slice of Dutch territory between Belgium and Germany, had to back down on his plans to move most of the cities shops directly to the border. 

See 

Program Notes for the MarijuanaNews World Report for May 24, 2005 Dutch NOT Closing Shops To Foreigners. Benefit of Sativex: Quacks Can’t Ignore Cannabis. Philippines Replace Cannabis with Tobacco. 

The other Dutch problems come from hard drugs. There are a number of “problematic” addicts, who probably have other mental problems, and are sometimes arrested for behavioral problems, but not for possession. If they behave too badly, they can be banned from the central city, but there is not a lot of violence associated with small-time retailing of hard drugs, perhaps because the Dutch generally don’t target small time dealers. 

There is not much violence in the wholesale cannabis business, but it is not unknown. However, there is more violence associated with wholesale trafficking of hard drugs for both the Dutch market and for export. Rotterdam is the largest European ports, so it is not surprising that it is also the entry point for contraband, but so is Antwerp, Belgium. 

On the other hand, nothing in Western Europe can begin to compare with what is happening just across the US border with Mexico. The problems that the Dutch have with their neighbors are nothing when compared with the problems Mexico has with its neighbor. Ten days ago, I wrote about the carnage in Juarez and Tijuana. But it only gets worse. 

See 

Drug War Carnage In Mexico Grows As Dozens of Bodies Found In Buried Mass Graves Just South of El Paso. At Least 3,000 Thousand More Killed Since 2006. 

Today, Reuters is reporting that murders in Juarez, “have flared to unprecedented levels.” “Some 200 people have been killed in drug violence in Ciudad Juarez so far this year, a tenfold increase over 2007, some shot dead on busy avenues or strangled after being tortured. Over the Easter weekend alone, 22 people were murdered in the city.” 

American critics of the Iraq war often complain that we do not pay sufficient attention to how many Iraqis have been killed. I think that American critics of the Drug War should place more emphasis on how many Mexicans and Colombians and others are being killed in our other war.

However, so long as the Mexican government tailors its policies to please its American supported prohibitionist ideologues, it will never be free of the violence. 

For historically obvious reasons, Mexican nationalism is focused on maintaining its sovereignty against North Americans, so it is particularly ironic or just absurd that they are so completely subservient to the US in the one area that is doing them more harm than anything else we have done in the last 150 years. 

Mexico has every right under international law to opt out of the various “drug” treaties, and there really isn’t anything that the US could do about it. Mexico could approach the Dutch and other European countries, seeking their support against “US imperialism.” I think that the Spanish government would be very receptive. 

See 

As More and More Countries Begin to Question Cannabis Prohibition, The Debate Should Be An International. Basic Rights Versus Toothless Treaties. Analysis by Richard Cowan 

There is no way the 

US we can hurt Mexico without seriously hurting the American economy. (It is our third largest source of crude oil – well over a million barrels per day. Canada is our largest So exactly how are we going to punish them? By cutting off the pipelines and walking to the unemployment office?) 

Even if the US still insists on waging the Drug War, Mexico could legalize marijuana and set up “coffee shops”. Then it could medicalize hard drugs, so that the distribution system would be completely legal up to the border. That would fundamentally change the nature of the smuggling business, and put most of the Mexican profits into the white market. There might still be some violence in the border cities, but the government could concentrate its resources there, because the violence – and corruption – in the interior would disappear. See 

Prominent Dutch Anti-Prohibitionist Agues That Cannabis Reformers Should Not Advocate Intensifying the War on Users of Other Drugs As An Alternative to Cannabis Prohibition. 

Unfortunately, both Canada and Mexico are governed by prohibitionists and the Mexican American community seems to be generally supportive of the Drug War. 

However, that does not relieve any of the rest of us from the moral responsibility to speak out about the carnage that our other war is inflicting on our vulnerable neighbor.
